title: Soda Farls
subtitle: Irish soda bread cooked as flat rounds on a griddle
excerpt: Irish soda bread made into a flat round and cooked on a dry griddle or frying pan, then split into four farls (quarters). Ready in 20 minutes with no yeast, no oven, and no kneading.
sourceNotes: Florence Irwin, Irish Country Recipes (1937), soda bread and griddle farls as staples of Irish domestic cooking. The soda farl is the griddle-cooked version of Irish soda bread and forms part of the Ulster Fry. Mrs Grace Mulligan and Cathal Grimes, Farmhouse Cookery (1981), soda farls documented as a Northern Irish daily bread.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze cooled farls in a sealed bag. Defrost at room temperature and warm in a dry pan for 2 minutes per side.
recipe.batchNotes: Double or triple the batch easily.

content.text: Soda farls are Irish soda bread cooked as a flat round on a dry griddle rather than baked in the oven. The dough needs bicarbonate of soda and buttermilk to rise: no yeast, no waiting, no kneading. The farl (from the Gaelic word for fourth) is cut into four quarters before cooking. Each quarter has a flat base, two cut sides, and a curved edge.
Mix {{plain-flour}} of plain flour, {{bicarbonate-of-soda}} of bicarbonate of soda, and {{sea-salt-fine}} of salt in a large bowl. Make a well in the centre and pour in {{buttermilk}} of buttermilk.
Mix with a knife or your fingers until just combined. The dough should be soft but not sticky. Do not overwork it: bicarbonate starts reacting with the buttermilk immediately.
On a lightly floured surface, pat the dough into a round about 20 cm across and 1 cm thick. Cut into four equal quarters with a sharp knife.

Heat a heavy, dry frying pan or griddle over medium heat. Cook the farls for 8 to 10 minutes per side until they are well risen, the cut surface has a dry crust, and a skewer inserted into the centre comes out clean.

rows.symptom: Farls are dark outside but raw inside
rows.fix: Lower the heat to medium or medium-low and cook for longer. Soda farls need time for the heat to penetrate to the centre.

rows.cause: Dough overworked, or bicarbonate not mixed in evenly, or buttermilk too cold
rows.fix: Mix until just combined and cook immediately. Do not leave the dough to rest.

rows.symptom: Dough is too wet to handle
rows.fix: Add flour a tablespoon at a time until the dough is soft but manageable. Different flour absorbs liquid differently.
Measure accurately. Bicarbonate of soda needs to be fully neutralised by the acid in the buttermilk; excess bicarbonate tastes bitter.

content.text: Soda farls are a staple of Northern Irish cooking and form part of the Ulster fry alongside bacon, eggs, sausages, and potato bread. They are less common in the Republic, where soda bread is more usually baked in the oven. The griddle version is faster: from mixing bowl to table in 30 minutes. The farl is eaten warm, split open, and buttered, or used to mop up egg yolk from a fried egg. It does not keep well and is best eaten on the day it is made.
